info.label: UMe
info.desc: Pretty Hate Machine (also known as Halo 2) is the first studio album by Nine Inch Nails. It was released on October 20, 1989 by TVT Records in the US, and on October 12, 1991 in the UK, and was a huge success. The first single off of the album, Down In It, was released on September 27, 1989. It received radio airplay for the aforementioned single as well as subsequent singles Head Like A Hole and Sin. The former also serves as a companion remix album of sorts to Pretty Hate Machine. Working nights at Right Track Studio as .

podcast.body: This album was Trent Reznor's debut record for TVT Records. The label owner, Steve Gottlieb, initially thought he was signing a "dancing technopop band" like Depeche Mode, but found the music too "heavy, too dark, too loud, too angry," describing it as an "abortion." Despite the label's initial distaste, they issued the record, and it sold half a million copies, largely through word of mouth. The album was later allowed to go out of print by TVT Records, making copies very hard to get. "Because Steve had spent so much recording it, TVT issued the record anyway and much to his surprise the records sold quite well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album was recorded in England in 1989 when Trent Reznor was 24, with limited time, budget, and studio knowledge. Although it sounded good at the time, studio technology had significantly advanced by 2010. Due to complex legal issues, the album was out of print for years, as Reznor couldn't access the original master recordings. "It was recorded in England in 1989. Trent had limited time, a limited budget and a limited knowledge of how to use a recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: Released on November 29, 1989, this album was initially hated by the label, TVT, and received no interest from MTV, commercial radio, or even the nascent alternative radio. Despite this lack of support, it sold over 150,000 copies in 14 months, which was considered impressive given its grassroots success. The album marked a shift for Trent Reznor from his earlier techno-pop influences towards a harder, more sinister industrial sound, incorporating elements of rage and fury inspired by bands like Ministry and Skinny Puppy. It was recorded by Trent largely alone in The Right Track studio during off-hours, with the help of four different producers in England who guided him in toughening up the sound. "Pretty Hate Machine was released on November 29, 1989, and that's when things started to get very strange."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
